text:
QUEEN
’
S BENCH FOR SASKATCHEWAN

Citation:
2013 SKQB
340

Date:
2013

09 19

Docket:
Q.B.G. 1133 of
2007

Judicial Centre:
Regina

BETWEEN:

PATRICIA HORNER

PLAINTIFF

-
and -

HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN
IN RIGHT OF

SASKATCHEWAN and THE WORKERS’ COMPENSATION BOARD

DEFENDANTS

Counsel:

Gordon Kuski, Q.C. and
Philip Gallet
for the
plaintiff

Leonard Andrychuk,
Q.C.
and Khurrum Awan                               for the
defendant,

Workers’ Compensation Board

Alan Jacobson                                                                                       for
the Crown

JUDGMENT
SCHWANN J.

September 19, 2013

INTRODUCTION

[
1
]
The Workers
’
Compensation Board (WCB), supported
by Her Majesty the Queen in Right of Saskatchewan (Saskatchewan), apply
pursuant to former Rule 188 of the former
Queen
’
s Bench Rules
for a determination of four separate
issues on questions of law. A determination of the points of law in favour of
the defendants will either dispose or substantially dispose of Ms. Horner
’
s action.

[
2
]
This case concerns a claim brought by
Patricia Horner who falls within a group or category of individuals often
referred to as
“
pre-
Charter
widows
”
. By operation of provincial workers
’
compensation legislation, Ms. Horner
lost her benefits as a spouse of a deceased worker upon her subsequent
remarriage in 1980. Following the introduction of the equality provisions under
the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
(
“
Charter
”
) on April 17, 1985, and with the
enactment of subsequent remedial workers
’
compensation legislation in
Saskatchewan,
“
post-
Charter
widows
”
no longer lose their survivor
’
s benefits upon remarriage.

[
3
]
Those legislative changes, however,
had no effect on Ms. Horner
’
s situation. Aside from a single
ex gratia
payment,
Ms. Horner
’
s benefits were not restored by the province
’
s remedial legislation. She brings
this action for declaratory relief pursuant to
s. 52
of the
Constitution
Act, 1982
, being Schedule B to the
Canada Act 1982
(U.K.), 1982, c.
11, and for reinstatement of her survivor
’
s benefits retroactive to April 17,
1985.

FACTS
AND LEGISLATIVE HISTORY

[
4
]
Patricia Horner and Brian Horner were
married on December 10, 1960. Brian Horner was killed in a workplace accident
on September 14, 1970. As a
“
surviving spouse
”
Ms. Horner was entitled to survivor
’
s benefits under
The

Workers
’
Compensation Act,
R.S.S. 1978, c. W-17, then in force
(the
“
1978 WCB Act
”
).

[
5
]
Ms. Horner remarried on September 19,
1980. Her remarriage engaged the operation of s. 68(1) of the
1978 WCB Act

which expressly triggered a one time lump sum payment equivalent to two year
’
s worth of benefits in lieu of
ongoing monthly payments. Section 68 provides:

Marriage of surviving spouse

68
. (1)      If a surviving dependant spouse marries,
the monthly payments to the spouse shall cease but the spouse shall be entitled
in lieu of them to a lump sum equal to the monthly payments for two years.

...

[
6
]
Although Ms. Horner subsequently
divorced her second husband, her previous benefits were not restored and she
remained disentitled to further benefits under the legislation.

[
7
]
On April 17, 1985,
s. 15
of the
Charter

came into force. Broadly stated, s. 15 guarantees individuals equality before
and under the law, and the right to equal protection and benefit of the law,
free from discrimination.

[
8
]
Recognizing the discriminatory nature
of legislation like s. 68(1) of the
1978 WCB Act
, provincial
jurisdictions across Canada took legislative steps to deal with the obvious
Charter

problems. Many jurisdictions simply reinstated benefits for affected widows,
back-dated to April 17, 1985. Saskatchewan
’
s initial legislative response was
the addition of s. 98.1(4) and (5) (
The

Workers
’
Compensation Amendment Act
,
1985
,
S.S. 1984-85-86, c.
89
) (
“
1985 WCB Act
”
). These provisions expressly provide
that, notwithstanding any other provision of the
Act
, compensation
payable to a surviving dependent spouse is payable regardless of whether the
spouse remarries. Significantly, though, the remedial effect of s. 98.1(4) was
limited by s. 98.1(5) to surviving spouses who remarried
after
the
amending legislation came into effect on September 1, 1985. The subsections
provide:

98.1(4)     Notwithstanding any
provision of
The
Workers
’
Compensation Act
and subject
to subsection (5), compensation payable to a surviving dependent spouse
pursuant to that Act or this section is payable regardless of whether that
spouse remarries.

(5)           Subsection (4)
applies only to surviving dependent spouses who remarry on or after the date
this section comes into force.

[
9
]
This section implicitly applied to
those like Ms. Horner who received compensation under the
1978 WCB Act
.
(
See
Ravndahl v Saskatchewan
,
2007 SKCA 66
,
299 Sask. R. 162
, per Smith
J.A. at para 42)  In other words, surviving spouses like Ms. Horner who had
remarried
before
September 1, 1985, remained disentitled to benefits
they had previously lost upon remarriage. Nothing changed for her.

[
10
]
On March 11, 1999, the Government of
Saskatchewan enacted amendments to
The Workers
’
Compensation General Regulations,
1985
, R.S.S. 1985,
c. W-17.1, Reg 1, s. 16.1, which reinstated benefits for surviving spouses back
to April 17, 1985, being the date
s. 15
of the
Charter
came into effect.
Again, this change had no effect on Ms. Horner or those like her who had
remarried
prior
to April 17, 1985.

[
11
]
The final legislative initiative of
significance took the form of
The
Special Payment (Dependent Spouses) Act
,
S.S. 1999, c. S-56.01 (the
“
Special Payment Act
”
) (repealed by c. 23 of the
Statutes
of Saskatchewan, 2012)
in 1999. The purpose of this
Act
was to
provide a single lump sum payment of $80,000.00 as a gratuity to surviving pre‑
Charter

widows like Ms. Horner who had remarried before April 17, 1985. Entitlement to
this one time lump sum payment was contingent upon an application being made
within two years from the date the
Special Payment Act
came into force.
It was also contingent upon the applicant providing a release of all claims and
a waiver of future rights of action against Saskatchewan and the WCB.

[
12
]
The terms of the release and waiver
(set out below) were prescribed by regulation. (
The
Special Payment
(Dependent Spouses) Regulations
, R.R.S. c. S-56.01, Reg 1, Appendix, Form
A) Ms. Horner executed the release on June 18, 1999. She received the $80,000.00
payment on June 22, 1999.

[
13
]
Ms. Horner and two other pre-
Charter

widows commenced the within action on August 14, 2007 seeking to have it
certified as a class action. Their certification application was initially
deferred pending the outcome of an appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada in
Ravndahl,
supra
. When the certification application came back before this Court,
Wimmer, J. denied certification  (
2009 SKQB 270
,
336 Sask. R. 12
). He
concluded:

13            Clearly, the
plaintiffs' claims for personal relief are statute‑barred. Paragraphs 25
and 26 of the Supreme Court judgment in
Ravndahl, supra
, describes what
is left to be litigated:

[25]       The Court of Appeal unanimously upheld the
appellant's right to maintain her claims for a declaration under
s. 52
of the
Constitution
Act 1982
that the impugned legislative provisions were unconstitutional
insofar as they operated on discriminatory grounds,
2007 SKCA 66 (CanLII)
,
[2007] S.J. No. 282
.

[26]       It will be for the trial judge to determine
whether a declaration of invalidity should be granted, and if so, what remedies
if any should be granted. Because the appellant's personal claims are statute‑barred,
any remedies flowing from s. 52 would not be personal remedies, but would be
remedies from which the appellant, as an affected person, might benefit.

14            These remaining
issues can be more efficiently, economically and quickly dealt with as a single
claim rather than in a class proceeding which the balance of authority holds to
be an undesirable vehicle for the determination of constitutional questions. As
well, as I see it, a single proceeding would effectively achieve the same
result for all members of the class.

[
14
]
As a result of that decision, Ms.
Horner amended her statement of claim by striking all references to the other
two plaintiffs thereby making it her action alone. A Fresh as Amended Statement
of Claim was filed on April 17, 2012.

[
15
]
The crux of Ms. Horner
’
s claim is that s. 98.1(5)

of
the
1985 WCB Act
and the
Special Payments Act
are
unconstitutional and of no force and effect. She seeks a declaration of
constitutional invalidity pursuant to
s. 52(1)
of the
Constitution Act, 1982

in relation to those Acts along with
“
a remedy pursuant to s. 52(1) of the
Constitution
Act
being the reinstatement of their survivors
’
pension retroactive to April 17,
1985", plus interest and costs.

[
16
]
By way of background, and as alluded to
above, parallel proceedings were brought in this Court by Laura Ravndahl in
2004. Like Ms. Horner, Ms. Ravndahl was a pre-
Charter
widow. However,
unlike Ms. Horner, Ms. Ravndahl chose not to sign the release and did not
receive the $80,000.00 lump sum payment. Ms. Ravndahl commenced an action
against the defendants for a declaration that legislation relating to the
termination of dependent spousal benefits upon remarriage was unconstitutional.
She also sought relief by way of reinstatement of benefits, damages,
pre-judgment interest and costs.

[
17
]
The defendants in
Ravndahl

successfully applied to strike her claim on grounds it was barred by operation
of a limitation period. That decision was upheld on appeal in relation to Ms.
Ravndahl
’
s claim for personal relief only, but
her application for a declaration of constitutional invalidity survived.

[
18
]
The
Ravndahl
case ultimately
wound its way to the Supreme Court of Canada where in a decision rendered in
2009, the Supreme Court substantially upheld the Saskatchewan Court of Appeal
(
2009 SCC 7
,
[2009] 1 S.C.R. 181
). The significance of this decision to the
within application is discussed more fully below.

AGREED
STATEMENT OF FACT

[
19
]
For purposes of this motion, the
parties agreed to the following statement of facts and documents:

1.             On or about June 1,
1999, the WCB sent a letter to the Plaintiff enclosing an application form and
release form under
The
Special Payment (Dependent Spouses) Act
. Attached
as Exhibit
“
A
”
is a true copy
of the WCB letter dated June 1, 1999.

2.             The Plaintiff completed
the application form and executed the release and returned them to the WCB,
which received them on or about June 21, 1999. Attached as Exhibits
“
B
”
and
“
C
”
respectively
are true copies of the signed Application for Lump Sum Payment and Release.

3.             A lump sum of $80,000
was paid to the Plaintiff under cover of a letter from the WCB dated June 22,
1999. Attached as Exhibit
“
D
”
is a true copy of the WCB letter dated June 22, 1999.

[
20
]
The contents of the release executed by
Ms. Horner have direct bearing on the issues before this Court and it is
therefore set out in its entirety:

Appendix

FORM
A

Release

In this release,
“
released parties
”
means:

(a)         the Government of Saskatchewan and each of
its past and present ministers, officials, servants, agents and
representatives; and

(b)        The Workers
’
Compensation Board continued pursuant to
The Workers
’
Compensation Act, 1979
and each of its past and present officials servants,
agents and representatives.

I,
“
Patricia Horner
”

of           #404-606 Victoria Ave Saskatoon
[name]                                         [place of residence]

in consideration of the sum of
$80,000, release the released parties of and from all actions, causes of
action, claims and demands of every nature and kind whatever, including,
without restricting the generality of the foregoing, any claim I may have
pursuant to
The
Saskatchewan Human Rights Code
,
the
Canadian Charter
of Rights and Freedoms
and all rights to the past and future compensation or
benefits payable pursuant to
The
Workers
’
Compensation Act
that I ever had, that I now have or that my heirs, executors,
administrators or assigns or any of them may have arising out of the
suspension, discontinuance or termination of compensation or benefits payable
pursuant to
The Workers
’
Compensation Act, 1979
or
any former
Workers
’

Compensation Act
to me as a dependent
spouse or common law spouse of a worker who died prior to September 1, 1985 as
a result of an injury.

I also agree to immediately
discontinue any action, suit or proceeding of any kind in any court or before
any administrative body, including The Workers
’
Compensation Board and the Saskatchewan Human Rights Commission,
directly or indirectly against the released parties and will not now or at any
time hereafter institute, commence, maintain or assign any action, suit or
proceeding of any kind in any court or before any administrative body with
respect to the matters released.

IN WITNESS WHEREOF this RELEASE
has been executed on June 18, 1999 ...

ISSUES

[
21
]
By court order of December 19, 2012,
the following points of law were directed to be determined:

1.            Assuming for the purpose
of this application that subsection 98.1(5) of
The Workers
’
Compensation Act
, c. W-17.1 discriminates on the basis of marital status contrary to

subsection 15(1)
of the
Charter
, can the respondent
’
s claim be estopped or barred by the release executed
by the respondent on June 18, 1999? If so, are there any legal grounds on which
the release would not be enforceable?

2.            Do the respondent
’
s claims for declarations of invalidity set forth in
paragraph 40 of the statement of claim require an impermissible retroactive or
retrospective application of
s.15(1)
of the
Charter
and therefore
disclose no reasonable cause of action?

3.            Assuming for the purpose
of this application that
ss. 68(1)
of
The
Workers
’
Compensation Act
, R.S.S. 1978, c. W-17 was inconsistent with the
Charter
, does
ss. 98.1(5) of
The Workers
’
Compensation Act, 1978
, c.
W-17.1 discriminate on the basis of marital status contrary to
ss. 15(1)
of the

Charter
?

4.            Are the respondent
’
s claims in paragraph 41 of the statement of claim
barred by
The Limitations Act
, S.S., c. L-16.1?

ANALYSIS

1.              Is
Ms. Horner
’
s claim estopped or barred by the release she executed
in favour of the defendants?

[
22
]
As discussed above, entitlement to the
one time $80,000.00 lump sum payment under the
Special Payments Act
was
conditional upon the applicant furnishing the WCB with
“
a release in the prescribed form
”
. (s.3(c)). The core issue before
this Court is whether the document signed by Ms. Horner releases the WCB and
Saskatchewan from her action and all claims and demands made thereunder. This
issue can be distilled into two sub-issues:

a.            Is it possible to waive a claim based on
a past infringement of a
Charter

right? and

b.            If so, is the release a valid waiver of
Ms. Horner
’
s right to bring this action?

[
23
]
Before delving into these issues, it is
important to note that Ms. Horner has not and does not contend that the special
payment and associated release were unconscionable, obtained under duress or by
fraud or misrepresentation. Neither does she claim to have failed to understand
the form of release which she executed.

a.         Is
it possible to waive a claim based on a past infringement of a
Charter

right?

[
24
]
Assuming ss. 98.1(5) of
1985 WCB Act

discriminates on the basis of marital status contrary to
s. 15
of the
Charter
,
Ms. Horner contends the Government cannot legislate a scheme to abrogate her
Charter

rights. According to Ms. Horner, where a government seeks to avoid the
protections of the
Charter
, it must utilize the "notwithstanding
clause" set out in
ss. 33(1)
of the
Charter.

[
25
]
Ms. Horner further submits that her
Charter

protected rights cannot be waived, and in any event the prescriptive nature of
the terms of payment, enshrined in provincial legislation, left her powerless to
negotiate its terms. In consequence, she submits, she did not and could not
freely give up her
Charter
rights.

[
26
]
The defendants contend Ms. Horner is
estopped from pursuing her claim by the release she executed on June 18, 1999.
The release represents an agreement between the parties to settle a potential
Charter

claim. In substance, it constitutes a release and waiver of claims, not a
waiver of a
Charter
right.

i)       waiver of
Charter
rights

[
27
]
The parties agree
Syndicat
Northcrest v. Amselem
,
2004 SCC 47
,
[2004] 2 S.C.R. 551
(
“
Amselem
”
) is the controlling authority on the
core issue of waiver of
Charter
rights. Both sides submit the case
assists their respective positions.

[
28
]

In
Amselem
, the appellant
erected a succah on his balcony in contravention of the condominium
co-ownership agreement he had signed. A succah is a temporary hut or booth
traditionally made of wood or other materials, open to the heavens, in which
Jews are commanded to dwell temporarily during the Jewish religious festival of
Succot.

[
29
]
The Supreme Court of Canada found the
impugned provisions of the declaration of co-ownership prohibiting construction
of succahs on balconies infringed the appellant
’
s freedom of religion as protected by
Quebec
’
s
Charter of Human Rights and
Freedoms
, R.S.Q., c. C-12 (
“
Quebec
Charter
”
). Based on the facts before it, the
court concluded the appellant had not waived his right to freedom of religion
nor did he implicitly agree not to set up succahs.

[
30
]

The reasons given in
Amselem

were threefold. First, there was no express prohibition against the
construction of succahs set out in the declaration of co-ownership, but rather
a constructive permission. This inherent ambiguity obviated any question of
waiver or implicit agreement on the part of the appellant. Second, the
circumstances presented to Mr. Amselem offered him no choice but to sign the
declaration of co-ownership in order to live at the condominium and
consequently he did not and could not validly waive his rights to religious
freedom. Third, the waiver in issue did not explicitly reference the appellant
’
s
Charter
rights. Justice
Iacobucci noted that
“
[a]t a minimum, waiver of a fundamental right such as freedom
of religion, if possible at all, presumably need not only be voluntary; it must
also be explicit, stated in express, specific and clear terms ...
”
. (para. 100)

[
31
]
While the conclusion reached
in
Amselem

appears on first blush to assist Ms. Horner, this decision must be read
carefully. To begin with, the case turned on the Quebec
Charter
and not
the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
. In this respect it cannot
be relied upon as a comprehensive analysis of
s. 15
of the Canadian
Charter
.
Second, for the reasons expressed above, the majority did not definitively
decide whether a waiver of constitutional rights was legally permissible and at
best concluded the issue was not free of doubt. At para. 92, the Court
observed:

92            Whether one can
waive a constitutional right like freedom of religion is a question that is not
free from doubt: see, e.g., for cases where waiver was disapproved of:
Insurance
Corp. of British Columbia v. Heerspink
,
1982 CanLII 27 (SCC)
,
[1982] 2 S.C.R. 145
, at p. 158
;
Ontario
Human Rights Commission v. Borough of Etobicoke
,
1982 CanLII 15 (SCC)
,
[1982] 1 S.C.R. 202
;
Newfoundland
Association of Public Employees v. Newfoundland (Green Bay Health Care Centre)
,

1996 CanLII 190 (SCC)
,
[1996] 2 S.C.R. 3
, at para.
21
;
Parry Sound (District) Social Services
Administration Board v. O.P.S.E.U., Local 324
,
[2003] 2 S.C.R. 157
,
2003
SCC 42
, at para.
28
. But see where cases recognized waiver:
R. v. Mills
,

1999 CanLII 637 (SCC)
,
[1999] 3 S.C.R. 668
;
R. v. Rahey
,
1987 CanLII 52 (SCC)
,
[1987] 1 S.C.R. 588
;
R. v. Richard
,

1996 CanLII 185 (SCC)
,
[1996] 3 S.C.R. 525
;
Frenette v. Metropolitan Life Insurance Co.
,
1992 CanLII 85 (SCC)
,
[1992]
1 S.C.R. 647
.

[
32
]
It is of significance that all of the
cases
cited in
Amselem
,
supra,
which held against the legitimacy
of a
Charter

waiver involved provincial human rights legislation and all
concerned a purported waiver or contracting out of
prospective
human
rights.(
Insurance Corp. of British Columbia v. Heerspink,
1982 CanLII 27 (SCC)
,
[1982] 2
S.C.R. 145
;
Ontario (Human Rights Commission) v. Etobicoke (Borough)
,
1982 CanLII 15 (SCC)
,
[1982]
1 S.C.R. 202
;
Newfoundland Association of Public Employees v. Newfoundland
(Green Bay Health Care Centre)
,
1996 CanLII 190 (SCC)
,
[1996] 2 S.C.R. 3
,
[1996] S.C.J. No. 54,
(QL)
;
Parry Sound (District) Social Services Administration Board v. Ontario
Public Service Employees Union, Local 324 (O.P.S.E.U.)
,
2003 SCC 42
,
[2003]
2 S.C.R. 157
. More to the point, the infringements which formed the basis of
the litigation in each instance had not yet occurred when the waivers were
signed.

[
33
]
The WCB and Saskatchewan submit
Amselem

and the referenced line of cases are distinguishable
from Ms. Horner's
situation in one fundamental respect: the impugned release in Ms. Horner
’
s situation does not seek to waive
Ms. Horner's
s.15(1)

Charter

rights on a go-forward basis. Instead, by
its terms, Ms. Horner has purportedly released the defendants from
past

Charter

infringements and also waived her ability to sue in the future based on the
discontinuation of her WCB survivor benefits in 1980. As the termination of
benefits occurred in the past, the document signed is not a waiver of future infringements
but part and parcel of an overall settlement of
Charter
litigation.

[
34
]
The decision in
Chow v. Mobil Oil
Canada
,
1999 ABQB 1026
,
[1999] 12 W.W.R. 373
is cited by the defendants for
the proposition that the principle against  release of prospective
Charter

violations does not extend to settlements for past acts of discrimination.
In
Chow
,
the plaintiff had signed a waiver releasing her employer from all actions,
claims and demands relating to the termination of her employment relationship
which arose after she informed her employer she was pregnant.

[
35
]
The Alberta Court of Queen's Bench
concluded that while "...one cannot contract out of future rights under
human rights legislation, unless the result is to advance or improve on the
rights provided by the
Act
", a release for past infringements is
not unlawful. (para. 46). The Court concluded at para. 67:

[67]    ... However,
I am of the view that a release of past alleged acts of discrimination is not a
contracting out, as that term has been used by the Supreme Court. The
fundamental difference is that the type of release I have been referencing has
no application to future discriminatory acts and is a settlement concerning
only an alleged past breach of the Act. Additionally, a release applies
exclusively to the signatory, not to employees generally.

[
36
]
(See also
Ermineskin Cree Nation v.
Foureyes,
2005 ABQB 522
,
382 A.R. 215
,
Barton v. Rouge Valley Health
System
,
2010 HRTO 2126
,
[2010] O.H.R.T.D. No. 2125 (QL)
(Ont. Human Rights
Tribunal)
,
Perricone v. Fabco Plastics Wholesale (Ontario) Ltd.
,
2010
HRTO 1655
,
[2010] O.H.R.T.D. No. 1652 (QL)
(Ont. Human Rights Tribunal)
)

ii)      covenant not to sue

[
37
]
Another distinguishing feature between
the document signed by Ms. Horner and the circumstances
in
Amselem
, supra,
rests
in the fact Ms. Horner covenanted not to commence an action in the future in
consideration of the lump sum payment.  Specifically, she agreed:

...not now or at any time
hereafter institute, commence, maintain or assign any action, suit or
proceeding of any kind in any court or before any administrative body with
respect to the matters released.

[
38
]
The
“
matters released
”
, to which the covenant applies,
refers to the specifics contained in the preceding paragraph of the release,
that is the suspension, discontinuance or termination of benefits as a
dependent spouse of a worker who died prior to September 1, 1985 as a result of
an injury.

[
39
]
Again, she did not waive a prospective
Charter

right
per se
but instead purported to waive
her right to litigate

the termination of her benefits.

[
40
]
On some level one might argue that a
right without a remedy is no right at all. Put another way, it could be
legitimately asked how the principle which prohibits waiver of
Charter

rights could assist Ms. Horner (to the extent it applies in this case) if she
has no remedy for its breach by reason of the covenant not to sue. That
argument, I believe, is squarely met by the fact she expressly waived her right
to sue for past
Charter
violations stemming from the termination of her
survivor
’
s benefits before September 1, 1985.

[
41
]
This line of reasoning was considered
in
Adbusters Media Foundation v. Canadian Broadcasting Corp.,
2009 BCCA
148
,
92 B.C.L.R. (4
th
) 9
and
R. v. Glaister,

2004 O.T.C. 34
,

[2004] O.J. No. 112 (QL)
(Ont. Sup. Ct.)
. Both decisions appear to provide
judicial acceptance for a lower threshold in relation to covenants not to sue
for
Charter
breaches as opposed to a waiver of the
Charter
right
itself. As stated in
Glaister
:

[13]     But a
breach already having occurred, the right to waive a claim to a remedy stands
upon a somewhat different footing. Some may conclude that this observation is a
distinction without as difference, but as John Donne observed in a famous
devotion, "no man is an island entire of itself". Denial of
Charter

rights to one person, even with that person's express consent, may affect
others, diminishing the superordinate social values we cherish and the
integrity of the judicial process. The denial of
Charter
rights may also
otherwise impact directly upon others.

[15]     On the
other hand, the accused's failure to claim a
Charter
remedy may not have
such far reaching effects. It may impact upon the accused only.
A breach
having already occurred the defence may make a tactical decision not to claim a

Charter
remedy and this should be respected
. (
R. v. Rees

(1994)
1994 CanLII 1372 (ON CA)
,
19 O.R. (3d) 123 (C.A.)
). [Emphasis Added]

[
42
]
Similarly, in
Adbusters, supra,

where the British Columbia Court of Appeal grappled with an alleged violation
of freedom of expression contrary to
s. 2(b)
of the
Charter
, Donald J.A.
opined that a waiver made in the context of a settlement offer could prevent a
defendant from being added to a
Charter
action. (His comments were
arguably
obiter
as the matter was remitted back to the trial court for
consideration on the substantive issues.)

iii)     waiver
of
Charter
rights in the criminal context

[
43
]
It has long been recognized in the
criminal law context that an accused may waive procedural safeguards provided
the waiver is clear and unequivocal. As stated in
Korponay v. Canada
(Attorney General),
1982 CanLII 12 (SCC)
,
[1982] 1 S.C.R. 41
,
132 D.L.R. (3d) 354
:

... the validity of
such a waiver, and I should add that that is so of any waiver, is dependent
upon it being
clear and unequivocal that the person is waiving the
procedural safeguard and is doing so with full knowledge of the rights the
procedure was enacted to protect and of the effect the waiver will have on
those rights in the process
.
...
[emphasis in original]

[
44
]
Waiver of procedural and due process
rights enshrined in the
Charter

has been recognized in the following
circumstances:

●

R v. Rahey
,
1987 CanLII 52 (SCC)
,
[1987]
1 S.C.R. 588
,
[1987] S.C.J. No. 23 (QL)
and
R. v. Askov
,
1990 CanLII 45 (SCC)
,
[1990] 2 S.C.R.
1199

[1990] S.C.J. No. 106 (QL)
- waiver of right to be tried within a
reasonable amount of time guaranteed by s. 11(b);

●

R. v. Richard
,
1996 CanLII 185 (SCC)
,
[1996]
3 S.C.R. 525
,
[1996] S.C.J. No. 43 (QL)
- waiver of right to be tried by an
independent and impartial tribunal guaranteed by s. 11(d);

●

R. v. Tran,
1994 CanLII 56 (SCC)
,
[1994]
2 S.C.R. 951
,
[1994] S.C.J. No. 16 (QL)
- waiver of right to the assistance of
a translator guaranteed by s. 14;

●

R. v. Evans,
1991 CanLII 98 (SCC)
,
[1991]
1 S.C.R. 869
,
[1991] S.C.J. No. 31 (QL)
and
R. v. Smith
,
1991 CanLII 91 (SCC)
,
[1991] 1 S.C.R.
714
,
[1991] S.C.J. No. 24 (QL)
- waiver of right to counsel guaranteed by s.
10(b);

●

R. v. Borden
,

1994 CanLII 63 (SCC)
,
[1994] 3 S.C.R. 145
,
[1994] S.C.J. No. 82 (QL)
- waiver of protections against
unreasonable search and seizure guaranteed by s. 8.

[
45
]
The WCB submits Ms. Horner
’
s argument, when viewed in the
context of  criminal proceedings and its procedural protections, leads to a
specious result. If the law fails to recognize a validly executed waiver of a
previously implicated
Charter
right in a civil context, how can it be
squared with the legitimacy of a waiver of existing
Charter
’
s
rights where an individual
’
s liberty is at stake. In other
words, Ms. Horner should not be permitted to disavow herself of a conscious
decision to waive
possible pre-existing
Charter
violations when
the law goes so far as to recognize the right of an accused person facing
jeopardy to waive
existing

Charter
protections. This argument, in
my view, has considerable merit.

iv)      policy considerations

[
46
]
Both defendants underscore the policy
implications presented by Ms. Horner's position. Counsel for Saskatchewan makes
the point that Ms. Horner's position, if accepted, would make it impossible for
any government agency with responsibilities based on the
Charter
to
enter into settlement arrangements with potential litigants who advance
Charter

based claims. If a citizen is not able to release a government agency from a
claim based on an alleged
Charter
violation, disputes could not be
settled and all disputes would of necessity proceed to trial.

[
47
]
Such a result, in my view, would be
contrary to the values of finality and certainty that litigation settlement is
intended to promote. On the one hand are the interests of the government
defendants, which are in no different position than other litigants in the
sense they must balance risk, competing interests and finite resources in
crafting an appropriate litigation strategy. Removing the possibility of a
binding release would effectively fetter the government's ability to settle
Charter

based claims. It is worth noting that releases provided in favour of public
bodies and governments have been held to be enforceable and bar the subsequent
legal proceedings contemplated by the terms of the release agreement.
Subsequent legal proceedings commenced in the face of a binding release have
been found to be an abuse of process. (
Roussy v Red Seal Vacations Inc
.,

2011 SKCA 116
. 377 Sask. R. 68,
Marble (Litigation Guardian of) v.
Saskatchewan
,
2003 SKQB 282
,
236 Sask. R. 14
)

[
48
]
Equally so, WCB submits an inability to
enforce settlement agreements in circumstances like Ms. Horner
’
s is, in the long run, adverse to the
broader public interest as it will serve as a strong disincentive against
compensation for moral claims which are perceived to be legally weak. With the
spectre of future litigation hanging in the air, absent an enforceable and
binding release, settlement would not be in the public interest.

[
49
]
The plaintiff
’
s position must also be considered.
She, too, must weigh the pros and cons of settlement with an eye to the same
considerations as the defendants with  risk of outcome playing a significant
factor. Like all plaintiffs, Ms. Horner bears the burden of proving her claim,
and like all litigants, there is no certainty of victory. The settlement offer
enshrined in the
Special Payment Act
gave her an opportunity to receive
compensation (albeit far less than what she wanted) without incurring lengthy
and costly court processes, and perhaps more importantly, without risk. After
all, Ms. Horner has not yet established a
s. 15
violation, nor is there
certainty she would be granted the relief sought even if she prevailed.

v)       the
“
notwithstanding
”
clause

[
50
]
The plaintiff submits Saskatchewan
should have invoked the notwithstanding or override clause contained in
s. 33

of the
Charter
as opposed to making a special one time payment
conditional on release. She submits that since none of the impugned legislation
invoked s. 33, the government cannot successfully say the
Charter
has no
application to those laws.

[
51
]
Section 33 enables governments to
override specified
Charter

protected rights (including
s. 15
equality
rights) and thereby be free from the invalidating effect of those provisions.
“
...The override power, if exercised,
would remove the statute containing the express declaration from the reach of
the
Charter
provisions referred to in the declaration without the
necessity of any showing of reasonableness or demonstrable justification
”
. (Peter W. Hogg,
Constitutional
Law of Canada
, 5
th
ed, looseleaf,  (Toronto:Carswell, 2007) vol.
2, at p 39-2) The practical effect of this legal principle is that the override
would insulate the statute from judicial scrutiny.

[
52
]
With that legal backdrop in mind, I
turn to the flaws in Ms. Horner
’
s argument. First, the suggestion government must invoke a s.
33 declaration in this circumstance to override
s. 15
of the
Charter
is
premised on the underlying assumption that Saskatchewan knew the legislation
was
Charter
non-compliant, yet purposefully proceeded to enact just such
a law in the face of this legal reality. To be clear, for purposes of this
application alone, a
Charter
infringement has been assumed for the sake
of argument. There is no evidence Saskatchewan enacted the impugned legislation
knowing full well the legislation was constitutionally flawed. Furthermore, as
Saskatchewan submits, the impugned legislation is remedial in nature inasmuch
as it was designed to address and respond to a perceived
Charter
issue
which solidified when s. 15 of the
Charter
came into force.

[
53
]
Second, there appears to be no
authority for the proposition that a government
must
invoke the
notwithstanding clause in every occasion where
Charter
protected rights
are involved. While it is true that invocation of s. 33 insulates legislation
from
Charter
attack and judicial scrutiny, there is nothing which
requires governments to legislate this provision into statute. Surely
governments have the legislative freedom to enact what they perceive to be
constitutionally sound legislation. By opting not to invoke s. 33 (the
legislative norm in Canada), government merely exposes the legislation to the
possibility

of a
Charter
challenge but whether that challenge has merit and can
succeed is another matter entirely. Ironically for Ms. Horner, had the
government invoked the notwithstanding clause as she suggests they should, her
claim would have been foreclosed and  beyond judicial review.

[
54
]
In conclusion, although there appears
to be judicial support for the proposition
Charter
rights cannot be
waived, the release in question does not purport to waive future or prospective
rights. Understood in its context, and with regard to the specific wording
employed, Ms. Horner both settled any claim she may have had for prior
Charter

violations and covenanted not to commence a
Charter
based action in the
future.

b)         Is
the Release a valid waiver of Ms. Horner's right to bring this action?

[
55
]
Ms. Horner contends the release does
not barr her claim because she did not freely waive her
s. 15(1)

Charter

rights. As there was no opportunity for negotiation owing to the prescriptive
nature of the release document, she contends that she "cannot in any
meaningful sense be taken to have freely  given up" her claim.

[
56
]
The defendants, on the other hand,
submit the release is clear, unambiguous and constitutes a complete bar to
these proceedings, including claims brought under the
Saskatchewan Human
Rights Code
, S.S. 1979, c. S-24.1 and the
Charter
. Its terms
expressly release rights to past and future compensation and benefits. Finally,
Ms. Horner expressly agreed by covenant not to commence an action.

[
57
]
Before examining the wording of this
document, it must again be underscored that Ms. Horner does not seek to
invalidate the release and waiver on ordinary principles of contract law. To
repeat, she does not contend the special payment and release were
unconscionable, obtained under duress or by fraud or misrepresentation. Nor
does she claim that she failed to understand precisely what she executed.

[
58
]

In
Amselem
, supra,
Iacobucci J.
articulated the hallmarks of a valid waiver. At para. 96 he observed:

96            Second,
by its very nature, waiver of any right must be voluntary, freely expressed and
with a clear understanding of the true consequences and effects of so doing if
it is to be effective:
see
Richard
, supra,
at para.
22
.

[
59
]
Iacobucci
J. expanded upon the concept of
“
voluntariness
”
with reference to that
Court
’
s decision in
Godbout v. Longueuil (City),
1997 CanLII 335 (SCC)
,
[1997]
3 S.C.R. 844
,
[1997] S.C.J. No. 95 (QL)
.
Godbout
involved a case where
the City of Longueuil made employment with it contingent upon employees signing
a written declaration agreeing to reside within the city confines. The
plaintiff was faced with the uncomfortable choice of either maintaining a
permanent residence in Longueuil for the duration of her employment or quitting
her job and seeking employment elsewhere. The court found the mandatory
residence requirement for city employees infringed s. 5 of the Quebec
Charter

and that the waiver was ineffective because the plaintiff had no real choice in
the matter. La Forest J.
in
Godbout

commented:

72            Indeed,
I find the appellant's contentions in respect of waiver to be entirely
unpersuasive, inasmuch as they fail to recognize that the respondent had no
alternative but to accept the residence requirement if she wanted to assume
permanent employment with the municipality. By its very nature, waiver or renunciation
of any right must be freely expressed if it is to be effective. Here, however,
the appellant simply presented the respondent with two possible options ‑‑
she could either relinquish her post entirely (or continue only in a temporary
capacity), or she could assume a permanent position as long as she undertook to
maintain her home in Longueuil for the duration of her employment. ...

[
60
]
Ms. Horner
’
s central argument is
simply this: her consent was not freely given and consequently not voluntary by
reason of the fact  she had no power to negotiate its terms. This position may
have sway if Ms. Horner i) was required to waive a prospective
Charter

right in exchange for compensation;  ii) faced stark alternatives; and iii) her
decision to accept the funds turned on the wording of the release.

[
61
]
As
discussed above, the release does not purport to waive prospective

Charter

infringements and in this respect it
is distinguishable from
Godbout
.
With regard to the
“
no alternative
”
argument, Ms. Horner
’
s situation stands in
contrast to both
Godbout, supra,
and
Amselem, supra
.
In
Godbout
,

the plaintiff could either sign the declaration and abide by the residency
requirement or lose her job.
In
Amselem
,
the appellant was required to
either sign the condominium agreement or find another place to live. In both
situations, the court found the alternatives unreasonable to the point of not
constituting a choice at all. In fact
in
Amselem
,
the court went so far
as to characterize the so-called choice as "insensitive and morally repugnant".
(para. 98)

[
62
]
While it is
true that Ms. Horner had no opportunity to negotiate the terms of the release
inasmuch as it was a prescribed form,
her alternatives were not quite so stark. She had two
choices. Either she could sign the release and accept the one time $80,000.00
payment, or she could refuse to sign and forego the lump sum payment. Refusal
to sign would give her the secondary options of either joining Ms. Ravndahl in
her claim, launching her own claim, or doing nothing at all.

[
63
]
Viewed in this context, Ms. Horner had
a choice of outcome and unlike
Amselem
and
Godbout
, it did not
require her to waive a
Charter

right but merely relinquish a potential
Charter

claim. Her decision to take the settlement was both tactical and strategic on
her part. There is no evidence before this Court that pressing financial need
dictated that choice. In short, there is nothing before this Court to undercut
the voluntariness of that decision. The fact she had no input into the wording
of the release document is in my view irrelevant and disconnected from her
underlying decision to accept the payment. It was her decision to accept the
settlement funds which must be viewed from the voluntariness perspective.

[
64
]
Other hallmarks of a valid waiver

articulated in
Amselem
are that it be explicit, clear and unequivocal. I
find the terms of this particular waiver to meet those requirements. According
to its terms, in consideration of receiving the $80,000.00 payment, Ms. Horner
released
“
...all actions, causes of action, claims and demands of every nature and
kind...
”
that she ever had, now has or may
have
“
...arising out of the suspension,
discontinuance or termination of compensation or benefits...
”
payable pursuant to workers
’
compensation legislation as a
dependant spouse of a worker who died prior to September 1, 1985 as a result of
injury.

[
65
]
The net is cast broadly and to ensure
there was no misunderstanding, the
“
action or claim
”
referred to was expressly said to
embrace:

.......any claim I may have
pursuant to
The
Saskatchewan Human Rights Code
, the
Canadian Charter
of Rights and Freedoms
.....

[
66
]
The final paragraph of the release also
bears on this analysis as it contains an express covenant on her part not to
commence an action or proceeding with respect to the released matters. In my
view the
“
released matters
”
must refer to the underlying basis for her claim, and not
the form of pleadings which bring it before a court or tribunal. The nub of her

Charter
claim, as clearly expressed by the terms of the release, is any
action
“
arising out of the suspension,
discontinuance or termination of compensation or benefits
”
payable pursuant to workers
’
compensation legislation as a
dependant spouse of a worker who died prior to September 1, 1985 as a result of
injury.  The sought after declaration under
s. 52
that s. 98.1(5) and the
Special
Payments Act
are invalid due to an unjustified violation of
s. 15
of the
Charter

falls squarely within the definition of
“
proceeding
”
.

[
67
]
The terms of the release are expressly
stated in clearly drafted terms. While Ms. Horner may have had no input into
the precise wording of the release document, she nonetheless took the
settlement funds freely and voluntarily. There is no evidence to suggest
otherwise.

[
68
]
For all of the aforementioned reasons I
find Ms. Horner's claim to be estopped or barred by the release executed by her
on June 18, 1999. Consequently her claim must be dismissed on this ground
alone.

GROUND
NO. 4

[
69
]
In the event I am wrong on issue No. 1,
this action can be partially resolved on the limitations of actions issue.

[
70
]
Both Saskatchewan and the WCB contend
Ms. Horner
’
s claim for
in personam
relief, enshrined in para. 41 of her Fresh
as Amended Statement of Claim, is barred by
The
Limitations Act
, S.S.
2004, c. L-16.1. Relief sought pursuant to para. 41 includes reinstatement of
her survivor
’
s pension retroactive to April 17, 1985, interest and costs. The
defendants submit the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada in
Ravndahl,
supra
, is definitive, on point and binding, and in consequence Ms. Horner
’
s claim for
in personam
relief
cannot survive.

[
71
]
In defending this line of attack, Ms.
Horner, too, invokes the authority of
Ravndahl, supra
. It is her
position the declaratory relief sought under para. 40 of her claim (
i.e
.
a declaration that s. 98.1(5) of
The Workers
’
Compensation Act
and the
Special Payment Act
are
unconstitutional) is untouched by the statutory limitation period. Similarly,
her claim for monetary relief contained in the subsequent paragraph of her
prayer for relief is insulated by the fact it is housed as a
“
...remedy pursuant to Section 52(1)
of the
Constitution Act
...
”
(para. 41). Section 52
constitutional remedies are diverse and innovative, and the potential for
retroactive relief (such as reinstatement of benefits) cannot be foreclosed,
she argues. Accordingly, it is Ms. Horner
’
s position consideration of the
limitations argument should be deferred until the
s. 52
remedies are determined
by this Court.

[
72
]
To properly address this issue, a
discussion of the
Ravndahl, supra,
case is in order. The facts in
Ravndahl

are largely similar to those concerning Ms. Horner save for one key difference.
Ms. Ravndahl
’
s workers
’
compensation survivor
’
s benefits ceased by operation of
prevailing legislation upon her remarriage in 1984. Like Ms. Horner, the
subsequently enacted remedial legislation did not assist her but unlike Ms.
Horner, Ms. Ravndahl declined to take the $80,000.00 lump sum payment.

[
73
]
Ms. Ravndahl sued. In her prayer for
relief (clauses 30(a),(b) and (c)) she sought to have the operative
Saskatchewan legislation declared constitutionally invalid, however, she went
on to specifically claim reinstatement of her spousal pension,  damages,
interest, and costs. To be clear, the declaration of invalidity in her case was
specifically plead under
s. 52
of the
Constitution Act, 1982

and no
reference was made to
s. 24
of the
Charter
in the context of her
“
personal claims
”
.

[
74
]
Gerwing, J.A., for the Court of Appeal,
was alert to this omission. She  observed:

23            The statement of
claim in this matter does not refer expressly to
s. 24
of the
Charter

but all of the authorities cited by the appellant here and below are s. 24
cases. The Chamber judge also refers only to cases concerning s. 24 and in her
conclusion says:

[15]       In contrast, s. 3 of the
Act
is an
enactment of general application in the Province of Saskatchewan and provides a
generous six year time period. In these circumstances, I find no reason not to
conclude that the plaintiff's action based on
s. 24
of the
Charter
is
subject to s. 3 of the
Act
. As the action was commenced outside the six
year limitation period, it is statute barred. Accordingly, the action stands
dismissed.

...

25            I take this claim
to be under s. 24 with respect to the relief in paragraphs (d) to (h) and
accordingly to be within the term "action" under
The Limitation of
Actions Act
. The claim of the appellant here is personal and monetary and
accordingly within the definition of "action" in the limitation
statute and accordingly, subject to it.

...

29            This case law,
the respondents suggest, shows that, in addition to being rarely if ever
available with a
s. 52
declaration, a s. 24 remedy is the only way to get the
personal remedies "as presented in its Amended Statement of Claim."
The rarity of availability is not central to the question as posed, but the
authorities are supportive of the need to use s. 24, which, as noted above,
would make it subject to
The Limitation of Actions Act
.

[
75
]
The Court of Appeal went on to hold
that even if a monetary remedy was possible under
s. 52
of the

Constitution
Act, 1982
, Ms. Ravndahl
’
s claim was nonetheless in the nature of a monetary claim. At
para. 30 the court said:

[30]          ...
the discretion of the Court which would here be appealed to is for a
quantifiable monetary remedy, that is, a personal claim. This again would fit
within the definition of "action" in
The Limitation of Actions Act
.

...

[
76
]
This decision was appealed to and
upheld by the Supreme Court of Canada (
supra
). In its treatment of
whether Ms. Ravndahl
’
s personal claims were statute barred, the Supreme Court
logically began its analysis by pinpointing when her cause of action arose,
that being April 17, 1985. McLachlin, C.J. for the court reasoned:

18            ...The appellant
was denied benefits pursuant to the operation of s. 68(1) of the 1978 Act.
However, she had no cognizable legal action upon which to base her claim until

s. 15
of the
Charter

came into force. On April 17, 1985 a claim that the
non-receipt of benefits pursuant to s. 68(1) of the 1978 Act discriminated
against her on the basis of marital status became actionable. ...

[
77
]
The Chief Justice went on to discount
Ravndahl
’
s argument that a new cause of action
arose with passage of the
Special Payment Act
on the basis of
under-inclusivity of this remedial legislation. She said:

20            This argument
cannot succeed. The appellant's cause of action must be based, as explained
above, on the unconstitutionality of the 1978 Act . Subsequent attempts by the
Legislature to lessen the discriminatory effects of legislation do not create a
new cause of action in her favour. The remedial provisions did not affect her
position in any way.

...

23            In this case,
there is but one cause of action which arose on April 17, 1985, when
s. 15
of
the
Charter
came into force.

[
78
]
In the result, Ms. Ravndahl
’
s personal claims were declared
statute barred.

[
79
]
That decided, the Supreme Court turned
its attention to Ms. Ravndahl
’
s claim for
s. 52
declaratory relief, and on this point
guidance was provided about the range and nature of
s. 52
remedies. The court
began by observing that if a declaration of invalidity is made by a trial
court,
“
...any remedies flowing from
s. 52

would not be personal remedies, but would be remedies from which the appellant,
as an affected person, might benefit.
”
(para 26) The distinction between
in
personam
remedies and
in rem
remedies follows at para 27:

27            It is important
to distinguish the appellant's personal, or
in personam
, remedies,
brought by her as an individual, from an
in rem
remedy flowing from
s. 52

that may extend a benefit to the appellant and all similarly affected persons.
As stated in the factum of the intervener the Attorney General of Ontario:

Where legislation is found to be unconstitutionally
underinclusive, the prospective remedial option chosen by the court might
extend the benefit at issue through severance or reading in, or it might
suspend the operation of the declaration of invalidity to allow the government
to determine whether to cancel, modify, or extend the benefit at issue. If the
unconstitutional underinclusive benefit is extended to include the
[appellant's]

Charter
claiman[t] group, whether through the court's
s.
52(1)
declaration or through government's response to the court's
s. 52(1)

declaration, the [appellant], like any otherwise eligible person [in the
claimant group], reaps the benefit of the
s. 52(1)
declaration, even if the
claimant does not obtain a personalized remedy from the court. [para. 45]

[
80
]
With that jurisprudential context in
mind, I return to Ms. Horner
’
s claim. As made clear in the Supreme Court
’
s decision in
Ravndahl, supra
,
Ms. Horner
’
s cause of action arose on April 17, 1985 when
s. 15
of the
Charter

came into effect. Her statement of claim, though, was not filed until April 14,
2007, more than twenty years after her cause of action arose. This length of
time is clearly outside the two year limitation period provided for in
The
Limitations Act
.

[
81
]
Ms. Horner contends that
notwithstanding this obvious time lag, her monetary claims (
i.e
.
reinstatement of benefits) should not be struck because it constitutes the
remedial offshoot of her s. 52 claim. Paragraph 41(a) of her statement of
claim, which sets out her prayer for relief, is relevant to this discussion:

41.           ...

a)          a remedy pursuant to Section
52(1) of the
Constitution Act
being the reinstatement of their survivors
’
pension retroactive to April 17, 1985 which is the
logical extension of the declarations set out in paragraph 72 above.

[
82
]
The language employed in Ms. Horner
’
s prayer for relief begs the question
of whether her claim is, in essence, one designed to address a constitutional
deficiency, and in so doing secure a global remedy for all pre-
Charter

widows. Alternatively, by specifically seeking reinstatement of survivor
’
s benefits (a monetary benefit
accruing to Ms. Horner) based on a fact pattern personal to her circumstance,
it has the gloss of an
in personam
claim. If so, it is vulnerable to
being struck on limitations grounds.

[
83
]
The distinction between remedies which
flow from the supremacy clause enshrined in
s. 52
of the
Constitution Act,
1867
, and
s. 24(1)

Charter
remedies offers some insight into this
issue. Professor Roach explains the nuances in his text, Kent Roach,
Constitutional
Remedies in Canada
, 2d ed., looseleaf, (Toronto: Canada Law Book, 2013) at
p. 14-1:

The Supreme Court has stressed
that
s. 52
provides remedies for laws that violate the
Charter
, whereas
s.
24(1)
provides remedies for governmental acts that violate the Charter. (
R.
v. Ferguson,
2008 SCC 6 (CanLII)
,
[2008] 1 S.C.R. 96
,
228 C.C.C. (3d) 385
, at para.
61
) Litigants
thus must determine whether impugned acts are specifically authorized by
statutes and as such require a
s. 52(1)
challenge, or whether they are acts
that are not authorized by legislation and that only require a s. 24(1) remedy.

Section 52(1)
remedies are distinct from s. 24(1) remedies because they provide
global remedies that are designed to cure the constitutional deficiencies in
the law going forward.

[
84
]
On the whole, its unclear if Ms. Horner
consciously eschewed a personal claim and personal relief in favour of a public
claim with a global remedy enuring to all affected persons. Perhaps its  merely
clever drafting on her part by attempting to bootstrap a s. 52 declaration of
invalidity to her monetized claim and thereby insulate it from a limitations
defence. The fact the relief sought in the statement of claim was crafted as
“
... a remedy pursuant to Section
52(1) of the
Constitution Act
being the reinstatement of
their

survivors
’
pension
”
lends credence to the former argument. On the other hand the word
“
their
”
may simply be a remnant from her
earlier attempt to certify it as a class action under
The
Class Actions Act
,
S.S. 2001, c. C-12.01.

[
85
]
I have determined none of these
questions need be answered in order to resolve the limitations issue. While it
would have been preferable to sever the discreet portions of Ms. Horner
’
s statement of claim which advance an

in personam
claim, that is simply not possible given the way in which
her statement of claim was drafted. Rather, it will be sufficient to resolve
issue no. 4 by declaring that any and all remedies sought by Ms. Horner of a
personal nature are statute barred and dismissed, and I so order.

’
